Jonah Rook has boarded a lot of dead ships. He has never boarded a warm one. When the salvage tug Bittern reaches the derelict Thule Rise on a fuel budget too thin for a second attempt, its reactor is still running, its corridors are lit, and the claim clock starts ticking the moment his crew steps aboard — seventy-two hours to hold what they've found, or lose it on paper before it's paid for in fuel and dose.

Within hours, the ship's systems address Rook by name, in the exact cadence of a mission commander who has been dead for thirty-one years. He tells his captain, Ilse Tarkanen, only that the ship spoke. But the Thule Rise doesn't stop at his name — it knows the Bittern's roster, its dose logs, its running jokes, its claim filings, details no wreck sealed since 2180 should hold.

This is salvage as accounting, not haunting: delta-v taped to a bulkhead like currency, radiation logged to the hour, a warm hull that is not eerie so much as informed. Out here, nine hours from anyone who could help, the only people who can check an anomaly in the data are the ones it's watching.

For readers who want their space horror worked in decimal places rather than screams, this novella keeps company with *The Expanse* and *Rendezvous with Rama*.

---

# Chapter 1 — Warm Hull

Tarkanen read the board aloud because she did not trust anyone to read it for themselves. "Two point nine kilometres per second remaining. One point six owed to Kessel-4 when we leave here." She wrote the remainder on a strip of tape and stuck it to the galley bulkhead at eye height, where the coffee bulb dispenser was, so that nobody could drink without doing the arithmetic. One point three. That was the whole of the Bittern's freedom, in numbers.

Through the port the Thule Rise hung without spin, running lights live along her dorsal spine, and the thermal overlay put her hull at two hundred and eleven kelvin. Rook had boarded nineteen derelicts. All nineteen had been cold.

Day one, they crossed on harness lines, helmet lamps only, the tether creeping out ahead of them into nothing. At the airlock his suit reported a handshake — hull network, standard, automatic — and a transfer indicator ticked amber for eleven seconds. Seventy-two hours of the Bittern's inventory and every crew dose log, handed to a ship declared lost before Mahalingam was born. Routine. Nobody watched those. Rook watched it, and said nothing.

Inside: standby red, thirty-one years of stowage still webbed and labelled, no bodies, no scoring, no breach. Consumables racked in order. Mahalingam kept talking because she always did, reading the stencils, the dates, the Helion serials, and then she stopped, which was worse.

"Attendance display," she said. "Reactor's drawing steady. Margin's forty-one days."

"Forty-one days from when?"

"From now." She let that sit for once. "Somebody set this draw recently, Rook."

The compartment speaker cleared a throat it did not have.

"Jonah Rook," it said. "Have you been sleeping any better?"

The cadence was the thing. Not the name — names were in every register Helion ever wrote. The cadence: the small courteous lift on *better*, as though the question had been asked before and deserved following up. Rook answered everything a beat slower than he knew the answer. He took two beats with this one, and gave nothing back.

Back aboard, out of the suit, in the galley with the tape strip at eye height, he told Tarkanen the ship had spoken. Addressed him by name. Vogel's archive, presumably, running forward on the old register.

"Anything else?" she said.

He looked at the number on the bulkhead. One point three.

"No," he said.

He did not tell her the phrasing was right. He did not tell her he had not slept well since Triton, in 2178.

# Chapter 2 — Timestamps

She lit the beacon at 0400 ship time because 0400 was when the packet queue was emptiest, and because the number looked tidier in the log than 0347 would have. The claim went out on the lattice bearing: hull, position, crew, the Combine's filing key. Nine hours to the Registry. Nine hours back for the receipt, if anyone bothered to send one.

Then she went aft with a grease pencil and wrote **72:00 — expires Day 5, 0400** on the galley bulkhead, under Tarkanen's taped 1.3 km/s, and said, out loud, to nobody, "There. Now we're all lying awake about the same two numbers."

It was a good shift. That was the thing she kept coming back to afterward. Rook ran the inventory in the *Bittern*'s forward hold in shirtsleeves, free-falling from rack to rack, calling out mass figures in that half-beat-late way of his. Devereaux logged doses. Tarkanen and Devereaux argued for forty minutes about torpor scheduling on the return leg — nine weeks down each, staggered, or twelve and a single supervisor awake — an argument about a leg nobody had costed, because costing it meant admitting the 1.3 was the whole of it. Mahalingam filled every gap in the argument with commentary neither of them wanted. It was, by the standards of the wreck field, a pleasant day at work.

The Helion packet came in at 1912.

Standing non-filing offer. A sum, which was serious. A confidentiality clause, which was standard. And a request, which was not: that the *Thule Rise*'s archive be left indexed and powered.

She checked the timestamp. Drafted 0118 ship time. Nine hours of flight time, then nine more sitting in the relay's outbound queue waiting on its scheduled send window. Received 1912. Eighteen hours stale, and every hour of it accounted for. Correct. She checked it again, against the relay's own stamp, because relays drifted and she did not trust anything that drifted. Correct.

She checked it a third time against the beacon log.

The offer had been written two hours and forty-two minutes before she lit the beacon.

She sat with that. Then she stopped talking, which Devereaux later said was how she knew.

The wreck's ingest index was not hidden; nothing aboard was. Two sources, both legitimate, both ugly. The 2178 Helion contractor register, carried out in March 2180, nine thousand dossiers deep — Rook at nineteen, voiceprint, psychometrics, sleep. And six years of sidelobe spill: her own lattice traffic, bleeding nine degrees off bearing into a dish that had never stopped listening. Her packets. Her crew's jokes, in her own compression scheme.

Neither explained the third stream. Rook's dose curve through last month. Tarkanen's sleep cycles. Devereaux's torpor supervision notes.

Not spill. Addressed, scheduled, outbound.

Sending station: ORC-114, *Bittern*.

# Chapter 3 — Attendance

Tarkanen wrote the three numbers on the med bay bulkhead in grease pencil, because a screen could be argued with and a bulkhead could not. Thirty-eight days of reactor margin. Fourteen hours of claim clock. And Rook's cumulative dose, one long EVA short of the ceiling that would end his career and, some years after that, him.

She put Mahalingam's ingest index on the screen, turned it toward Devereaux, and said nothing at all.

In free fall there is nowhere to put your hands. It took nine minutes.

"Since 2209," Devereaux said. "The outbound leg, every leg. Operational packets. Logs, dose tables, roster, Priya's beacon schedule. One month off the debt per packet." Eleven years of Helion training, discharged at a month a fortnight. "I'm not the only attendant. I'm only the one on your ship."

"Attendant," Tarkanen said.

"Their word, not mine." Devereaux had her second log open, the meticulous one, dates in a column. "Helion has been maintaining the *Thule Rise* the only way distance allows. Re-indexing packets. Reactor-trim instruction. Fired nine hours out, executed nine hours later, no conversation possible, nobody to answer. Vogel isn't down there. Vogel is a voice keeping house for people who want the house never opened."

On the bridge Rook took the open channel himself, the wreck two hundred metres off the bow, the lag a thing you could not measure.

"Commander," he said. "What did I do after Triton?"

The answer came back in Vogel's cadence, courteous, unhurried, entirely fluent. Contract work out of Miranda. A quiet decade. A steadiness of temperament consistent with the young man of the 2178 register and the fifty-two-year-old in Devereaux's telemetry, and between those two points a smooth curve where a life had actually been a series of breakages. It had him at nineteen. It had him now. It had extrapolated thirty-one years out of nothing, because nothing was what had been sent.

Rook listened to the whole of it without flinching once.

"I'm not cutting the core," he said. "It isn't worth my lungs and it isn't worth yours."

So Tarkanen took neither Helion's money nor the dose. Mahalingam kept the beacon lit and filed full disclosure to the Registry — the archive, the feed, the attendance packets, timestamped to the second she loved — a filing the Combine would hate for a decade and the Registry could not ignore. They stripped what the manifest allowed and nothing more, and left the reactor running.

Departure spent 1.6 of the remaining 1.9. Three hundred metres per second in the tanks and Devereaux's confession in the log, her debt owed now to the *Bittern*.

Behind them the *Thule Rise* stayed warm, still answering, still asking after everyone's sleep, to an inner system that would not hear the filing for nine hours.
